articles.title: The TXT record that exists in your panel but not in your zone
articles.excerpt: Domain verification looks like the simplest task in the book. A service hands you a record name and a value, you paste both into your DNS panel, you hit "verify". Then you spend an hour staring at a f…
articles.body: Domain verification looks like the simplest task in the book. A service hands you a record name and a value, you paste both into your DNS panel, you hit "verify". Then you spend an hour staring at a failure while the record sits right there in the table. Here is the failure mode I keep running into, and the one-line check that settles it. Your panel appends the domain Many hosting panels assume the name field holds a prefix only , and that they will append the zone name for you. The verifying service, meanwhile, gives you the fully qualified name: verification.example.com . Paste the full name, let the panel append the domain, and the zone ends up with verification.example.com.example.com . The records table looks fine, because the table shows what you typed.

articles.title: Is Your Eval Too Small?
articles.excerpt: Picture this: you spend an afternoon tweaking a prompt, run your 100-example eval suite, and watch accuracy jump from 80% to 83%. Three whole points. You merge the PR. The question I wanted to answer:…
articles.body: Picture this: you spend an afternoon tweaking a prompt, run your 100-example eval suite, and watch accuracy jump from 80% to 83%. Three whole points. You merge the PR. The question I wanted to answer: did you improve anything, or did you get lucky? To find out, I ran a simulation where System B is 3 points better than System A (true accuracy 83% vs 80%, using seeded NumPy draws across 5,000 runs per sample size, from 25 to 1,000 examples). On a 100-example eval, the truly better system tied or looked worse one run in three . The raw numbers are in output.txt and results.json , and the write-up is the README . A 50 to 100 example eval cannot tell a real 3-point gain from noise, and running both systems on the same examples is the cheapest fix available.

articles.title: Roblox Gerstner waves: getting the water height at a world point
articles.excerpt: If you render Gerstner waves and then ask "how high is the water at (x, z)", you get two different answers. The maths is usually correct in both places. The problem is that the mesh moves sideways and…
articles.body: If you render Gerstner waves and then ask "how high is the water at (x, z)", you get two different answers. The maths is usually correct in both places. The problem is that the mesh moves sideways and the query does not. This is about Luau and Roblox, but it holds for any engine with a choppy wave mesh and a separate water-height query. One caveat before the code: this is not a secret. A 2021 DevForum answer says it plainly: the formula "doesn't just return a new Y value. It also returns new X and Z values. When you ignore the X and Z values, it will appear out of sync." People have known for years.

articles.body: A pair of companies in Europe have signed an agreement to study the feasibility of developing weapons that can be dropped from orbit. Atmos, a space company known for its Phoenix reusable reentry vehicle , will work with MBDA, Europe's largest missile manufacturer, on the new project. "We are assessing how proven defense systems and new orbital technologies can be combined to strengthen Europe's conventional deterrence and enable future defense capabilities," Sebastian Klaus, the CEO of Atmos Space Cargo, said in a statement on Nov. 18. The system that the companies are investigating is called Precision Orbital Deep Strike, or PODS. The companies said that their initial scope will center on design and feasibility, as well as technology integration.

articles.title: Who turned the W upside down? Why Cassiopeia won't sit still
articles.excerpt: The queen in the northern night sky is supposedly one of the easiest constellations to recognize — you just look for a W. Or is that an M?
articles.body: Some constellations are like old friends. You know them well, they're always there, and they never seem to change. A case in point is Cassiopeia, the queen. Its beautiful name comes from Greek mythology — the mother of Andromeda — and its shape is said to represent a queen sitting on a throne. To a stargazer, Cassiopeia is best known as a prominent northern constellation shaped like the letter W. It's easy to find — look north, find five reasonably bright stars making a W, congratulate yourself on finding Cassiopeia and use it to get somewhere more interesting. It's so often a signpost, not a destination. But look north a few hours after dark this month, and you'll notice the W has gone.
